The Neolithic Revolution. A profound cultural and economic shift from hunter-gatherer subsistence to settled agricultural societies, beginning roughly ten thousand years ago in the Fertile Crescent and spreading globally. This transition—from foraging wild foods to deliberately cultivating crops and herding animals—restructured human society, enabling permanent settlements, population growth, social hierarchy, and the emergence of civilization itself.

Agriculture emerged independently in multiple regions. The Fertile Crescent, China, Mesoamerica, and elsewhere. This suggests it arose from common pressures rather than a single innovation. It was one of humanity's most transformative discoveries. But the adoption of agriculture was not immediately advantageous. Early farmers often experienced worse nutrition, more disease, and harder labor than contemporary hunter-gatherers, yet populations committed to farming spread because it supported higher population density.

Settlement and agriculture went hand in hand. Permanent villages like Jericho and Çatalhöyük arose as communities invested in cultivating specific plots of land, necessitating year-round residence and architectural stability. Domestication of plants and animals transformed human-environment relations fundamentally. Humans began reshaping landscapes for agricultural production rather than passively foraging. Selective breeding accelerated genetic changes in crops and livestock.

Social stratification emerged alongside agriculture. Storing surplus grain enabled full-time specialists—priests, warriors, administrators—creating class hierarchies unknown in egalitarian forager bands. Inequality became a defining feature of civilization.

Gobekli Tepe, in modern Turkey, complicates the narrative. Monumental architecture appeared nine thousand BCE, before agriculture, suggesting ritual and social organization preceded farming. This challenges the linear progression narrative. The Neolithic Revolution took thousands of years to fully unfold. The transition was gradual in most regions, with mixed economies of pastoralism and cultivation persisting for centuries or even millennia.

Population growth accelerated during the Neolithic. Sedentary settlement allowed higher birth rates since children were no longer constrained by the mobility demands of nomadic foraging life. Trade networks expanded. Agricultural surplus enabled specialization and exchange. Pottery, textiles, and other craft goods began circulating through incipient trade routes across the Mediterranean and Near East.

Environmental transformation preceded and accompanied agriculture. Forests were cleared, waterways diverted, and grasslands converted to cropland. The human footprint on the landscape became permanent and expansive. The Neolithic Revolution relates closely to early agriculture, the specific practices of crop cultivation and animal husbandry, and to domestication, the central technology enabling it all.
